summary: Describes using IKEv2 to negotiate security protocols and transforms for Fibre Channel as part of its Security Association Management Protocol. IKEv2 needs Fibre-Channel-specific protocols, transforms and name types, which this defines. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Fibre Channel is used to connect storage. This explains how a standard key-setting protocol can set up the secret handshake for it.

questions: how does fibre channel use ikev2
subtitle: Adapting IKEv2 to secure Fibre Channel networks

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel (a high-speed storage network) needs to authenticate devices and establish security associations, similar to how IKEv2 does it for IP networks. But Fibre Channel has different security protocols and message structures than IP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4595 specifies Fibre-Channel-specific extensions to IKEv2: new security protocol identifiers for Fibre Channel's ESP_Header and CT_Authentication, new transform algorithms, and a new address type for Fibre Channel names. This allows IKEv2 to negotiate security associations for FC without confusion with IP security.
tldr.outcome: Fibre Channel networks can use a standards-based, familiar key-negotiation protocol (IKEv2) adapted for their environment, and mixing IKEv2 for IP and Fibre Channel on the same network is made impossible by using different identifiers.

today: RFC 4595 is Informational and documents how the Fibre Channel Security Protocols standard uses IKEv2 for security association management. It has not been obsoleted. These extensions remain part of the FC-SP standard and are used in Fibre Channel implementations that require device authentication and encrypted traffic protection.

sections.title: Why Fibre Channel Needs Its Own Security
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is a gigabit-speed network technology standardized by the T11 committee primarily for storage networking. Unlike Ethernet, which is designed for general-purpose networks, Fibre Channel has dedicated protocols and frame formats for moving data between servers and storage arrays.

The Fibre Channel Security Protocols (FC-SP) standard defines a security architecture that provides device-to-device authentication, secret establishment, and data protection. To manage secrets and negotiate security associations, FC-SP adapted IKEv2, the Internet Key Exchange protocol used for IP networks. However, Fibre Channel's security protocols, transforms, and device identifiers differ from IP's. This document specifies those extensions so that IKEv2 can work for Fibre Channel without accidental confusion between IP-based IKEv2 negotiations and FC-based IKEv2 negotiations on the same network.
sections.eli5: Storage networks need to verify that devices are real and set up secret conversations. IKEv2 is a standard way to do this, but storage uses different formats than the Internet, so special codes are needed so each knows what the other is talking about.

sections.title: Fibre Channel Security Protocols
sections.content:
Fibre Channel defines two security protocols at different layers. ESP_Header (based on IP Encapsulating Security Payload, RFC 4303) protects FC-2 frames with origin authentication, integrity, anti-replay protection, and optional confidentiality. It is carried as an optional header in the FC-2 frame. The scope of authentication covers the entire FC-2 header and payload, with normalization of addresses (D_ID and S_ID) to allow for address translation in networks.

CT_Authentication protects Common Transport Information Units (CT_IUs) used for control traffic at the FC-4 level. It provides origin authentication, integrity, and anti-replay. The authentication uses a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA1-160 or HMAC-MD5-128) computed over the entire CT_IU except headers and CRC fields. Because data and control traffic are separate, only one protocol (either ESP_Header or CT_Authentication) applies to any single Fibre Channel Security Association.
sections.eli5: Storage traffic comes in two kinds: data and control messages. Each kind has its own way to add security protection. The data way is like wrapping a letter in an envelope with a seal. The control way adds a signature to prove the message is real.

sections.title: New IKEv2 Identifiers for Fibre Channel
sections.content:
To adapt IKEv2 for Fibre Channel, RFC 4595 allocates new identifier values in the IKEv2 registries.

ID Type: Fibre Channel entities are identified by an 8-byte Name (not IP addresses). A new ID type ID_FC_NAME (value 12) is defined to carry these names in the IKEv2 Identification Payload.

Protocol IDs: Security protocols are identified in the IKEv2 Security Association Payload. New values identify FC security protocols: FC_ESP_HEADER (value 4) and FC_CT_AUTHENTICATION (value 5). Deliberately not reusing the existing IP ESP value (3) prevents confusion and ensures negotiation failure if an IP endpoint accidentally meets an FC endpoint.

Transform IDs: For CT_Authentication, two new integrity transforms are defined: AUTH_HMAC_MD5_128 (value 6) and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 (value 7). These differ from IPsec's corresponding transforms by omitting truncation of the HMAC output: MD5 produces 128 bits (not 96) and SHA-1 produces 160 bits (not 96).

Traffic Selector Type: A new value TS_FC_ADDR_RANGE (value 9) defines Fibre Channel traffic selectors as lists of FC addresses and protocol ranges, rather than IP addresses and ports.
sections.eli5: IKEv2 uses numbered codes for different things: how to name a device, what kind of security, how to compute signatures, and what kind of traffic to protect. New numbers are assigned so Fibre Channel can use different formats without breaking IP's system.

sections.title: Using IKEv2 for Fibre Channel Security Associations
sections.content:
The Fibre Channel Security Association Management Protocol is a modified subset of IKEv2 (RFC 4306). It supports the basic IKEv2 exchanges: initial exchange to establish the IKE SA and first child SA, CREATE_CHILD_SA to negotiate additional SAs, and INFORMATIONAL exchanges (for notifications, deletes, and vendor IDs). Features not supported in FC include: negotiation of multiple protocols in one proposal, multiple outstanding requests, cookies, configuration payload, and the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP).

IKEv2 messages are carried over Fibre Channel using the FC AUTH protocol. A Fibre Channel Sequence can carry up to 4 GB of data, so there are no theoretical message size limits. However, some FC endpoints have limited sequencing capabilities, so the FC SA Management Protocol supports fragmentation of IKEv2 messages (as defined in the FC-SP standard). To minimize denial-of-service risks from reassembly buffer exhaustion, endpoints should use Hash and URL encodings instead of sending full certificates when possible.
sections.eli5: IKEv2 messages get packaged up and sent over Fibre Channel's wire format instead of IP. Most of IKEv2's basic features work; some advanced features that are only useful for IP networks are left out.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The security considerations of IKEv2 (RFC 4306) apply to Fibre Channel IKEv2, with exceptions for features that do not apply. NAT traversal and EAP are not supported by the Fibre Channel Security Association Management Protocol, so those IKEv2 security considerations do not apply. IP fragmentation is not a concern because Fibre Channel does not use IP.

The main security risk is denial-of-service via reassembly buffer exhaustion if an attacker sends fragmented IKEv2 messages that are not completed. Endpoints should limit reassembly resources and prefer Hash and URL encodings over certificates to keep messages short. The use of distinct protocol identifiers for Fibre Channel (4 and 5, not IP's 3) ensures that any accidental mismatch between an IP-based and FC-based IKEv2 peer will be detected as a negotiation failure, preventing subtle security issues from crossed protocols.
sections.eli5: Fibre Channel IKEv2 follows the same security rules as IP's IKEv2. The main protection is that if an IP system tries to talk to an FC system, they will immediately recognize they are incompatible and stop, preventing confusion.
